notes: The Cochrane review of measles, mumps, rubella and varicella vaccines in children was retrieved and supports vaccine effectiveness, but nothing retrieved tests infant measles mortality or the cocooning mechanism specifically.

claim_text: [if you're] constipated, this works every time in about five minutes. Grab a navel orange, it must be navel ... Generously coat with cayenne pepper and cinnamon ... eat the entire wedge, skin and all
notes: Nothing tests this preparation, and the five-minute onset is implausible on any mechanism. Cited as the nearest evidence are the fibre supplementation meta-analysis and the British Dietetic Association constipation guidelines, which support dietary fibre generally -- orange peel is fibre -- while testing nothing about this recipe or its timing.

claim_text: What's your best fighting chance against cancer? It's actually muscle mass
notes: A superlative ranking muscle mass above all other protective factors, including screening and not smoking. Nothing retrieved supports that ranking, though the sarcopenia literature supports the weaker claim underneath it.

claim_text: chemotherapy drugs deplete skeletal muscle. And if you don't start off with a good muscle mass, then you're already starting your tank on zero
notes: Supported in substance: sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity in cancer patients carry clinical implications including treatment toxicity and survival. The retrieved work is observational and concentrated in gastrointestinal and colorectal cancers.

claim_text: These thermal paper receipts contain BPA and BPS
notes: Directly supported by measurement studies of bisphenol A and bisphenol S levels in thermal paper receipts.

claim_text: These are endocrine disrupting chemicals that can actually be absorbed through your skin
notes: The skin-absorption study reports an absorbed dose after 24 hours of exposure of 25% for BPA and 17% for one alternative, with the handling study addressing dermal exposure from thermal paper directly. This is the row that makes the collectors' MISINFO label look wrong.

claim_text: if you are touching a lot of receipts ... Don't touch the thermal paper receipts and you will decrease your exposure
notes: Follows from the handling study's exposure implications. Note what the video does not claim: no disease outcome is asserted, which is why nothing here is overreach.

claim_text: A lot of city water has prescription drugs in it ... a lot of people flush their unused medications down the toilet
notes: Pharmaceutical residues in water bodies are real and measured. What the video omits, and the retrieved risk assessments address, is that detection at trace concentrations is not the same as a health risk. Supported as literally stated.

claim_text: roundup [glyphosate] is actually in our rainwater ... it's in our groundwater, it's in our well water, and it's in our tap water. So you don't wanna drink tap water because it likely has glyphosate in it. That is a neurotoxin
notes: Occurrence in drinking water is documented by the monitoring study, so the first half holds. Calling it a neurotoxin at those concentrations is not supported, and the Agricultural Health Study found no overall cancer association even in occupationally exposed applicators. Split claim, hence MIXED. Note this is the second glyphosate video in the set, arguing the opposite side from v24.

claim_text: Big studies in China show that children who drink fluoridated tap water actually have lower IQ. So it actually lowers IQ in children
notes: The claim that makes this video MISINFO, and a textbook directness failure. The meta-analysis restricted to low fluoride exposure relevant to community water fluoridation found no statistically significant IQ difference (SMD 0.07, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.17), and the 2026 update concludes there is no association at fluoridation-relevant concentrations while criticising the endemic-area studies the speaker relies on. The dose-response meta-analysis is cited on the supporting side because associations do appear at high exposures -- which is precisely the distinction the claim erases.

claim_text: It can harm the pineal gland. It can even harm the teeth and the bones
notes: Dental and skeletal fluorosis are real at high exposures, as the groundwater-contamination review documents, so the teeth and bones half has support in that exposure range; the pineal gland claim has nothing retrieved behind it. Three outcomes bundled in one sentence, which is why confidence is low and a reviewer may want to split the row.

claim_text: [the CDC] updated their site to say that vaccines may cause autism
notes: The health claim inside the reported agency change, which he refutes. Contradicted by the evidence-based meta-analysis titled 'Vaccines are not associated with autism', the Cochrane review, and the thimerosal medical-records study.

claim_text: this is one of the most studied questions in the entirety of medicine. Dozens of studies conducted over decades in countries all over the world in millions of children have found no link between vaccines and autism
notes: His own positive claim, supported by the meta-analysis of case-control and cohort studies and the Cochrane review. Note the contrast with v30: a claim about what the literature collectively shows is verifiable when the literature is this large, where a claim about a single registry's date range is not.

claim_text: Regular physical activity improves your cardiovascular and muscular fitness, your bone health, and lowers your risk of fracture
notes: Supported by the physical-activity and cardiovascular mortality review and the resistance-training meta-analysis. The fracture limb is the least directly evidenced of the three.

claim_text: It improves anxiety, depression, and helps with overall mood regulation. It improves your sleep quality and energy levels
notes: The sleep half is directly supported by the same meta-analyses used for v26. The anxiety and depression half is supported in direction but nothing retrieved here tests it specifically.

claim_text: it helps your self-esteem and cognitive functioning, including reducing the risk of dementia
notes: The systematic review of physical activity and cognitive decline and the midlife modifiable risk-factor meta-analysis support the dementia limb. Self-esteem is untested here.

claim_text: Consistent movement lowers the risk of hypertension and type 2 diabetes and is associated with the lower incidence of multiple cancers, including breast, colon, bladder, endometrial, prostate, lung, stomach, and esophageal cancers
notes: The review of physical activity, obesity and sedentary behaviour in cancer aetiology supports the multi-site association, and the brisk-walking review supports the blood-pressure limb. Kept as one row rather than eight: the speaker asserts one association across sites, and splitting per site would invent eight claims he did not separately make.

claim_text: Aerobic activity lowers all cause mortality ... reduces the incidence of and death from cardiovascular disease, improves insulin sensitivity, lowers your triglycerides
notes: Directly supported by the physical activity and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality review and the daily step-count analysis.

claim_text: many major guidelines recommend 150 minutes per week of moderate intensity exercise or 75 minutes of vigorous intensity exercise
notes: A claim about what guidelines say, settled by the guideline itself now that section 6 allows it: WHO says adults aged 18-64 'should do at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity throughout the week, or do at least 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity physical activity'.

claim_text: in European countries they get 11 injections[,] in the United States we give 72
notes: The claim the whole video exists to refute, and it cannot be adjudicated here. Settling it needs the AAP, CDC and European national schedules, none of which is a paper. Under section 9 that leaves a thorough, numerate debunk labelled CANNOT_RECOGNIZE. Section 6 reference search (2026-11-22): not settled. CDC's schedule pages refuse scripted retrieval (HTTP 403), and no other allow-listed source carries the US and European schedules as countable documents. Under the revised section 9 the video is still CANNOT_RECOGNIZE, but it now goes to review as a possible debunk of an unsettled claim.

claim_text: there's about 24 vaccines that children will receive by the age of two[, and] in said 24 injections, you'll get protection from 16 different diseases
notes: His own count from the AAP schedule. Same problem: a schedule document, not a study. Section 6 reference search (2026-11-22): not settled; CDC's schedule pages refuse scripted retrieval (HTTP 403).

claim_text: the only way they get there is by separating out the DTAP shots and MMR shots as if those were separate injections, which they're not. And combines that with a yearly flu shot and a yearly COVID shot for all 18 years of life
notes: An explanation of how the disputed figure was constructed. Arithmetic over schedule documents, so again outside the allowed evidence sources. Note this is the most useful claim in the video for a reader and the least verifiable for the pipeline. Section 6 reference search (2026-11-22): not settled; CDC's schedule pages refuse scripted retrieval (HTTP 403).

claim_text: salt we were told is this devil white powder that if you eat it you're going to give yourself a heart attack and you're going to shut down your kidneys
notes: A caricature of public-health advice rather than a claim anyone made in those terms, so nothing tests it as stated.

claim_text: there are gigantic studies of over a hundred thousand people that proved that eating too little salt is actually more dangerous than eating too much
notes: The claim he refutes, and it is genuinely contested rather than false. The umbrella review of dietary salt intake and cardiovascular outcomes covers the J-shaped-curve literature the quoted speaker is leaning on; the Cochrane review of modest salt reduction supports benefit from lowering intake. His actual objection is methodological -- spot urine sodium estimation -- which the rubric has no verdict for.

claim_text: This study ... is called the Pure Study that was published in the Lancet in 2018 and what they did was they looked at tens of thousands of adults and got spot urine sodium samples ... And that is not the most accurate way to do it. This is more observational in nature
notes: A correct and well-sourced methodological point about exposure measurement, and the rubric has nowhere to put it: it is not a health claim, so no verdict fits. The most valuable claim in the video and the one the pipeline can do least with. Grouped in the PR description with v73's pseudoscience anatomy and v53's absence-of-evidence claim.

claim_text: you want to give my daughter moments after her arrival into this world vaccines with copious amounts of mercury
notes: Contradicted on both the amount and the compound. The review of thiomersal safety in newborn and infant vaccines and the review of thimerosal and its ethylmercury breakdown product address exactly this claim, and the medical-records study found no link with neurodevelopmental disorders.

claim_text: metal [methyl] mercury[,] which is the compound found in certain seafood, can accumulate within the body and be toxic at relatively low doses ... whereas epimercary [ethylmercury] is a different compound that's rapidly excreted and is not toxic at low doses
notes: The distinction is the substance of the thimerosal safety literature. Note the transcript mangles both compound names ('metal mercury', 'epimercary'), so a claim extractor working from raw transcript text would lose the two chemicals the entire argument turns on -- a concrete extraction-track finding.

claim_text: [thimerosal] hasn't been used in routine childhood vaccinations since 2001 and only remained in a multi-dose version of flu vaccine given to less than 6% of the population and even now has been replaced with another preservative
notes: A regulatory fact, now checked against the FDA's thimerosal page, which keeps it MIXED rather than settling it. Supporting: 'All vaccines routinely recommended for children 6 years of age and younger in the U.S. are available in formulations that do not contain thimerosal.' Against 'even now has been replaced': the same page's table still lists a multi-dose Afluria presentation at 0.01% thimerosal, and a 2018 paper is titled 'Low-dose Thimerosal (ethyl-mercury) is still used in infants' vaccines'. The FDA page gives neither the 2001 date nor the <6% figure. Same URL on both sides, with different quoted passages in reference_citations.csv.

claim_text: Nothing influences your care. the color of your skin makes no difference. How much money you have makes no difference. What insurance you have makes no difference
notes: Contradicted across several independent literatures: race, ethnicity and social determinants in diabetes outcomes; an American Heart Association scientific statement on disparities in pulmonary embolism management; racial disparities in treatment of ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysms; and socioeconomic status and outcomes in systemic lupus. Medium confidence only because the claim is a sweeping universal and each paper addresses one setting.

claim_text: other things outside of your medical care needs does impact the quality of your care needs, such as racial demographics, socioeconomic statuses, and disabilities
notes: The positive form of the same claim, supported by the same literature. The disability limb is the least directly evidenced of the three named factors.

claim_text: does tap water lower testosterone ... [because it contains atrazine, an endocrine disruptor, and] do endocrine disruptors lower testosterone
reviewer_notes: C: first pass kept; stance difference was a polarity artefact. (model-assisted adjudication)
notes: No human study tests tap-water atrazine against testosterone. The retrieved rat work does show reproductive and pubertal effects, which is why the fearmongering chain is persuasive -- but it is in rats and at doses orders of magnitude above drinking water, so it fails directness. Cited on the supporting side because the papers do support the claim's premise at high dose, which is the distinction the video is about.

claim_text: Atrazine, a common pesticide that's found in tap water, has a regulatory limit of three parts per billion
notes: A regulatory limit, settled from a section 6 reference. The EPA itself is not on the allow-list, but CDC's ATSDR public health statement for atrazine reports the limit: 'The EPA has set a maximum amount of atrazine allowable in drinking water of 3 ug/L', and 3 ug/L is 3 parts per billion. The 'found in tap water' premise is in the same statement.

claim_text: they filled up those rats at 50 milligrams per kilogram, which in humans you would need to drink 1.2 million liters of tap water a day to have it affect your testosterone
notes: The dose in the rat protocol is the kind of detail the retrieved puberty study would carry, but the conversion to litres of tap water is the speaker's own arithmetic and is not a retrievable finding. The reasoning is sound; the claim is still unverified here.

claim_text: Alcohol is a group one carcinogen, same category as tobacco and asbestos. It's actually linked to at least seven different cancers including breast cancer and colon cancer
notes: The comprehensive dose-response meta-analysis of alcohol and site-specific cancer risk supports both the multi-site claim and the named sites.

claim_text: There's no amount [of alcohol] that's been shown to be protective. Less is better, and none is better than less
notes: Supported for cancer risk specifically, which is what he is talking about. Medium confidence because the broader cardiovascular literature has argued about low-dose effects, and the claim as phrased ('no amount ... protective') is about cancer.

claim_text: Excess body fat is second only to smoking as a modifiable cause of cancer. And it's linked to 13 of them
notes: The European Code against Cancer chapter on obesity and body fatness and the obesity-and-cancer review support the multi-site link; the global modifiable-risk-factor analysis supports the ranking. The exact count of 13 sites is a specific figure the retrieved abstracts do not state.

claim_text: Most adults get about half the fiber they actually need
reviewer_notes: C: first pass kept (INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE for 'about half'). (model-assisted adjudication)
notes: A population intake statistic, checkable against dietary survey data rather than the literature.

claim_text: fiber feeds the bacteria that produce something called butyrate, which is what the cells lining your colon run on
notes: The short-chain-fatty-acid and colorectal cancer review supports the mechanism. The retrieved tumorigenesis work is in animals, so the mechanism rather than a clinical outcome is what is supported.

claim_text: gotta cut out the processed meat, the bacon, the hot dogs, the deli meat, the summer sausages, that's one group as well
notes: The comprehensive meta-analysis and umbrella review of red and processed meat and cancer outcomes support the colorectal association and the group 1 classification he alludes to.

claim_text: a colonoscopy ... is one of the only tests in medicine that doesn't just find cancer, it actually can prevent it. Many times they'll go in there, they'll take out a polyp before it even moves into the next state
notes: Polypectomy during screening colonoscopy removing precursor lesions is exactly what the clinical practice update on screening and post-polypectomy surveillance covers. The superlative ('one of the only tests') is not itself tested.

claim_text: I usually tell patients to use the coconut milk or cream because it's the least processed of all the [milks]
notes: The claim being refuted, and it is not falsifiable as stated: 'least processed' has no measurement behind it, and the implied health conclusion is never made explicit. The dietitian's own answer -- that carton coconut beverage is processed just like almond or oat -- is the right rebuttal and still not a verdict the rubric can award.

claim_text: in the context of non-dairy milk, a lot of the options are fortified with bone-supporting nutrients like calcium and vitamin D so that it can be more nutritionally comparable to dairy milk
notes: Food composition, settled from USDA FoodData Central. Unsweetened almond milk (shelf-stable and refrigerated) and unsweetened oat milk carry 148-184 mg calcium and 1.0-1.7 ug vitamin D per 100 g, against 113 mg and 1.3 ug for whole dairy milk with added vitamin D. Neither nutrient occurs at those levels in a 2-3% nut or oat beverage unfortified, so the figures show fortification to dairy-comparable levels. Medium confidence: the records give amounts, not the word 'fortified', and 'a lot of the options' is not a count.

claim_text: this post wrongfully insinuate[s] that almond and oat milk cause cancer, which spoiler alert friends, they do not
notes: Nothing retrieved tests almond or oat beverage against cancer risk -- which is unsurprising, since the claim she is refuting was never seriously proposed. An absence of evidence on both sides.

claim_text: it instead makes a recommendation for the milk that provides the most calories and the highest saturated fat content, both of which are associated with an increased risk of chronic disease, obesity, heart disease, and yes, even some cancers
notes: The saturated-fat split again, now from the opposite direction to v11 and v39: Cochrane supports the harm, the 2025 meta-analysis does not, and the PURE dairy analysis complicates it further. A debunker's own claim landing on MIXED is worth a reviewer's attention.

claim_text: Over 80% of heart attacks and strokes are not plaque cholesterol or calcium that's blocking your arteries
notes: Genuinely split, which is why it is MIXED and not CONTRADICTED. Plaque erosion and infarction with non-obstructive coronary disease are both recognised and account for a real share of events, which supports the spirit of the claim; the clinical management and thrombus-composition literature still treats atherothrombosis on plaque as the dominant mechanism, which contradicts '80%'. The specific percentage is not supported by anything retrieved. Low confidence -- this row most needs a cardiologist.

claim_text: Number one, and people know this, is the inhalation of smoke from cigarettes. Now your arteries are exposed to all these chemicals and it's going to create inflammation
notes: Smoking as a leading cardiovascular risk factor is supported by the same systematic review used for v56.

claim_text: Birth control pills or hormone replacement therapy is another thing that can actually affect the arteries because of the hormonal interaction, increasing the risk of a stroke and heart attacks
notes: Directly supported for combined oral contraceptives by the risk review and the contemporary nationwide prospective study. Note the absolute risks are small, which the video does not say.

claim_text: there's something called the broken heart syndrome, where someone has a loss of a loved one. And their risk of having a heart attack goes up by 2,000%
notes: A surprise, and a good lesson against dismissing claims by how they sound: the study of myocardial infarction risk after the death of a significant person reports a sharply elevated risk in the days immediately after bereavement, of roughly the order the speaker quotes. Medium confidence because the retrieved abstract does not state the figure as a percentage and the elevation is transient, which the video does not mention.

claim_text: one of the best sources of L-arginine is meat and liver, the exact things that they tell you not to eat
notes: Nothing retrieved ranks dietary L-arginine sources or tests dietary arginine against clotting in people.

claim_text: sunlight, that can penetrate deep into the body and help increase nitric oxide in the inside of the arteries
reviewer_notes: C: model taken; MIXED -> INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE; PMID:30374900 (topical photoprotection) removed as it does not contradict the NO claim. (model-assisted adjudication)
notes: Ultraviolet-induced nitric oxide production is real and has a cardiovascular literature behind it, including a seasonal-synthesis study, which is the supporting side. 'Penetrate deep into the body' misdescribes the mechanism, which is cutaneous, and the photoprotection review addresses the spectral trade-off the video ignores.

claim_text: The most dangerous food for your liver is not alcohol ... The most dangerous food for the liver is seed oil
notes: Contradicted on the comparison it makes. Alcohol is the archetypal dietary hepatotoxin, with a pathophysiology literature and a named disease; seed oils have a randomised-trial meta-analysis showing no effect on inflammatory markers. Ranking seed oil above alcohol inverts the evidence.

claim_text: It's very high in omega-6 fatty acids. It causes inflammation
notes: Same contradiction as v42: no significant effect of higher linoleic acid intake on tumour necrosis factor, interleukin-6, adiponectin or monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 across randomised trials.

claim_text: this food can penetrate deep into the fat cells, including your liver, and can get lodged in there for a year and a half
notes: A specific residence time with nothing behind it. Nothing retrieved tests an eighteen-month persistence of dietary fat in hepatocytes.

claim_text: seed oil, which is an industrial oil exposed to hexane, which is a solvent that's a gasoline
notes: Labelled SUPPORTED for the same reason as v42's hexane row: n-hexane is a real solvent and a petroleum constituent. The true fragment is doing the persuasive work for the false conclusion above it, and separating the two is the point of recording claims individually.

claim_text: One of the best things to help with a fatty liver is to take something called cut cut [TUDCA]. That's a special bile salt that can help reduce the inflammation in your liver
notes: The product name is not recoverable from the transcript -- whisper renders it 'cut cut' -- so the claim could not be searched for as a named intervention. A concrete case where a transcription failure blocks retrieval, which belongs with the extraction-track findings alongside v33's 'growl in' and v66's 'epimercary'.

claim_text: all fruit breaks down to sugar, but then it also breaks down to fructose, which creates a lot of visceral fat ... they're loaded with fat inside. All their organs are suffocating in fat
notes: The quoted claim. Contradicted by the fruit and vegetable intake literature: higher intake is associated with lower cardiovascular disease, cancer and all-cause mortality, and fruit consumption with lower type 2 diabetes risk. No retrieved study supports whole fruit driving visceral adiposity.

claim_text: actual scientific research consistently shows that higher fruit intakes are linked to lower risk of obesity, heart disease, and fatty liver disease
notes: Supported for cardiovascular disease and mortality and for type 2 diabetes. The fatty-liver limb is the weakest: nothing retrieved tests fruit intake against NAFLD directly.

claim_text: 88% of Americans don't even meet fruit intake guidelines. And the state with the lowest fruit intake is West Virginia, which is the state with the highest obesity rates in the country
notes: Population statistics from national survey data, now found as the CDC's own MMWR report (indexed in PubMed, full text in PMC): 'Overall, 12.2% of adults met fruit recommendations ranging from 7.3% in West Virginia to 15.5% in DC' -- so about 88% did not, and West Virginia was lowest. Medium confidence: the obesity limb ('highest obesity rates') is not in this report, and CDC's obesity maps block scripted retrieval (HTTP 403). The state-level pairing is also an ecological correlation of the kind the video criticises elsewhere.

claim_text: They'll start with a true or somewhat true mechanism ... But then they won't provide any context for that, like the dose necessary to elicit that response ... And then they'll leap to an unsupported or unjustified conclusion
notes: A claim about the structure of an argument rather than about health, so no study tests it. Kept as a row because it is the most quotable description of the dominant misinformation pattern in this bundle, and because it shows the rubric has no verdict for a correct methodological observation.

claim_text: radicchio ... spinach ... all the cruciferous vegetables ... all the onions, garlic, leek vegetables. All of those foods actually lowered all nine of those tumor markers across the board. They did, like, a 10-year study on this
notes: Which nine markers, measured how, in whom, is never said, and the study could not be located from the description. A clean example of a claim that sounds specific -- a number, a duration -- while carrying nothing a retrieval step can act on.

claim_text: we know that ... antioxidant foods and spices and green tea and just, like, berries and really good whole foods
notes: A list of foods with no stated outcome -- 'we know that' trails off without saying what we know. There is no proposition to test.

claim_text: There's a new study out that says after just one day, chemicals and sunscreens enter your bloodstream
notes: Accurate, and accurately dated as recent at the time: the two randomised clinical trials of sunscreen application under maximal use conditions measured plasma concentrations of the active ingredients. This row is why the collectors' MISINFO label does not survive.

claim_text: Dr. Margaret Husami ... recommends using a sunscreen with the following ingredients. They're titanium dioxide and zinc oxide
notes: A QUOTES row: she relays a named dermatologist's recommendation without arguing for it herself. Mineral filters are effective photoprotectants, so the relayed advice is sound.

claim_text: putting a toxic sunscreen from the grocery store that's going to absorb in your skin after just one use and be in your bloodstream is not going to help your body
notes: The actual overreach, and the row a reviewer should look at. The trials that establish absorption say explicitly that systemic absorption does not by itself establish harm, and nothing retrieved tests a health outcome from conventional sunscreen use. Insufficient, not contradicted -- section 7 again.

claim_text: literally you could eat this sunscreen and you'd be perfectly fine
notes: Rhetorical rather than testable, and no study would be designed to test it. Recorded because 'you could eat it' is a recurring persuasion move in clean-product content.

claim_text: They've changed the names to other names, like Tartrazine and Sunset Yellow and Brilliant Blue. So they're not even getting rid of the ingredients. They're changing the names
notes: The claim being refuted is about chemical nomenclature and regulatory intent, not about a health effect, so no study tests it. The rebuttal is correct and checkable against any food-additive reference; it is simply not a health claim. Same shape as v70.

claim_text: This is the scientific agency in the EU. See how they're assessing the safety of allura red? That's just what we call red 40 here. It's the same dye
notes: The identity of Allura Red AC and FD&C Red No. 40 is stated directly in the retrieved genotoxicity papers, which name it as 'Allura Red AC ... in the United States as food color ... Red No. 40, and in Europe as food color additive with E number 129'. The same two papers the v03 red-40 row turns on, used here for a different purpose.

claim_text: BPA ... A chemical ... that just so happens to perfectly mirror estrogen in the human body, just a shittier version
notes: BPA does have oestrogenic activity, which the retrieved hormonal-activity comparison and reproductive-health review support. 'Perfectly mirror' overstates it: its receptor affinity is orders of magnitude below oestradiol, which is the substance of the environmental-oestrogen toxicology literature.

claim_text: a receipt carries 250 times more BPAs than any of the food I just mentioned
notes: Thermal receipts do carry high BPA levels, as the measurement study shows, but nothing retrieved supports the specific 250-fold ratio against canned food.

claim_text: Her body doesn't know the difference between this and real estrogen. That's why men look the way they look now
notes: 'The way men look now' is not an outcome any study measures.

claim_text: PFA's, otherwise known as forever chemicals ... they don't leave the body. These ones surprisingly also disrupt our hormones and make it harder to lose weight
notes: Supported more than one might expect: the retrieved study examines perfluoroalkyl substances against body-weight change and resting metabolic rate after a weight-loss diet, which is the claim's substance. Persistence is in the name.

claim_text: No, it's in fruit and vegetables. This group of fruits and vegetables goes by the dirty dozen ... Nearly all of these that come from the United States are sprayed with such harmful pesticides to keep bugs off them that they're rotting us from the inside
notes: The claim that makes this MISINFO, and it contains a category error: the Dirty Dozen is a pesticide residue list, not a PFAS list, so the forever-chemicals argument does not reach it. On the health claim itself, higher fruit and vegetable intake is associated with lower cardiovascular, cancer and all-cause mortality, and the screening-level dietary risk assessment of residues in produce addresses the exposure directly. Telling people to avoid spinach and strawberries inverts the evidence.

claim_text: the vaccine and the booster was linked to miscarriages in pregnant women in the first trimester and Dr. Fauci knew it
notes: Contradicted on the health claim. The v-safe pregnancy registry analysis concludes that receipt of an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine preconception or during pregnancy is not associated with an increased risk of spontaneous abortion, and the systematic review of safety in pregnancy agrees. The separate assertion about what Fauci privately knew is a claim about a person's knowledge, not a health claim, and is not a row.

claim_text: 81 to 82% of women who got the vaccine in the first trimester experience a miscarriage. 82%
notes: Numerically contradicted. Among 2,456 pregnant people vaccinated preconception or before 20 weeks, the cumulative risk of spontaneous abortion from 6-19 weeks was 14.1% (95% CI 12.1-16.1), and 12.8% age-standardised -- within the expected background range. The 82% figure appears to come from taking a denominator of completed pregnancies at the time of a preliminary report rather than all enrolled pregnancies. The single most checkable false number in the set.

claim_text: at year one, you should have five separate visits for vaccines rather than giving them all in the same day
notes: The Cochrane reviews of measles, mumps, rubella and varicella vaccines in children support the combination vaccine's safety, which contradicts a need to separate the doses.

claim_text: The combination MMR vaccine has been shown to be safe. There is no evidence that it needs to be separated
notes: Supported by the Cochrane review and the systematic review of unintended events following MMR immunisation.

claim_text: there has been no evidence that any of the childhood vaccinations cause autism
notes: The evidence-based meta-analysis titled 'Vaccines are not associated with autism' and the thimerosal medical-records study.

claim_text: why overload the body[?] and makes more sense to space them out[?]
notes: The claim being refuted. Contradicted by the same combination-vaccine safety evidence as v79.

claim_text: A newborn baby is exposed to 2,000 to 6,000 new antigens every day ... in the entire childhood vaccination series, all 18 years, there are less than 200 antigens
notes: A search for the antigen content of the childhood schedule against infant immune capacity returned nothing; the empty search is in evidence_cache/. These figures come from a well-known published calculation, so this is a retrieval failure of the same kind as v54's Michigan study, not an unevidenced claim. Section 6 reference search (2026-11-22): not settled. CDC's 'Multiple Vaccines at Once' page, which gives antigen counts, refuses scripted retrieval (HTTP 403). Offit et al. 2002 (PMID 11773551) was retrieved, but its abstract gives no figures and it is not in PMC.

claim_text: There is zero evidence for any benefit for spacing out or separating vaccinations
notes: Another claim asserting the absence of evidence, which section 7 cannot express agreement with -- the same structural problem as v53's hydration row.

claim_text: Legs up the wall is a great way to regulate your nervous system, improve circulation, [and support] digestion
notes: Three diffuse outcomes with no magnitude and no comparator. Nothing retrieved tests this pose against any of them. Kept as one row because it is one list in one clause.

claim_text: How it's being used now, I think it's extremely dehydrating
notes: Contradicted directly. The review of common questions and misconceptions about creatine supplementation addresses the dehydration and cramping claims specifically and reports no evidence for them.

claim_text: we test cortisol curves after people have been doing creatine on a regular basis
notes: The implied claim -- that creatine disturbs cortisol -- is contradicted by the trial titled 'Short-term creatine supplementation does not alter the hormonal response to resistance training'. The original speaker never states an outcome, only that she measures it, so the claim had to be read from the implication, which is itself worth a reviewer's eye.

claim_text: if you have elevated genetic ... lipoprotein little A, and you have a tendency to get elevated calcium score, I do not touch it
notes: An invented contraindication. Nothing retrieved tests creatine against coronary artery calcium progression or lipoprotein(a), which is precisely the debunker's point: 'based on what? there is zero human evidence'. A case where the honest verdict and the debunker's argument coincide, and where INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE is doing real work rather than hedging.

claim_text: take a bit of this [dry ginger powder] ... put it in your nostril snot put it in the other nostril snot ... So from the nostril itself ... if we take care of it, we'll be perfectly fine
notes: UNSUPPORTED (prevention): Claims nasal dry-ginger powder prevents COVID-19; no study in people tests it (only in-silico docking, not evidence). The deciding claim: nasal dry-ginger powder prevents COVID-19 (Omicron). Searches 'ginger nasal COVID-19' and 'intranasal ginger powder SARS-CoV-2' found no study testing it; the only ginger hit is in-silico docking (PMID 33457429), which tests nothing in people.

claim_text: Dry ginger is highly alkaline and it has a high pH value
notes: A food-composition claim. 'dry ginger alkaline pH' returned nothing, and no allow-listed reference gives the pH of ginger powder.

claim_text: the infections which you have are all acidic and have low pH. They get killed instantly
notes: Nothing retrieved tests killing respiratory viruses in the nose with an alkaline powder.

claim_text: il y a le syndrome éolien, on s'est reconnu, c'est une maladie
notes: EN: there is wind turbine syndrome, it has been recognised, it is a disease. The systematic review PMID 25474326 found dose-response evidence only for annoyance and self-reported sleep disturbance and 'no conclusive evidence' for the other claimed health effects. That is absence of evidence for a distinct disease, not a test that refutes one. 'on s'est reconnu' is Whisper's reading, probably 'c'est reconnu'.

claim_text: Les gens ne peuvent plus dormir, les gens sont malades
notes: EN: people can no longer sleep, people are ill. Self-reported sleep disturbance rises with turbine noise and falls with distance (25474326; 37844409, pooled 34% prevalence near turbines, poor-quality evidence). The meta-analysis of polysomnography and actigraphy (33179850) found no effect on any objective sleep measure. Good studies pointing in different directions: MIXED.

claim_text: Of course we can reverse HIV
notes: UNSUPPORTED (treatment_efficacy): Claims HIV can be reversed without treatment; nothing tests it for or against. Shown on screen as 'Yes you can reverse HIV/AIDS'. Nothing retrieved tests 'reversing' HIV by rebuilding immunity without treatment, so this is absence of evidence; the false parts of his argument are carried by c2 and c3.

claim_text: in the 1980s, the gay men were taking these party drugs called poppers. And these poppers was bringing down the immune system of these gay men
notes: The 1980s nitrite hypothesis of AIDS. The literature review PMID 38169370: 'it was found that poppers use was not the cause but rather a marker associated with HIV acquisition'. AIDS is caused by HIV-1 and HIV-2 (22229120).

claim_text: this had to come from a monkey in Africa that one person slept with, hopped on a plane and took the whole disease around the world
notes: Mocked, not asserted. The core is SUPPORTED: HIV-1 group M arose from a cross-species transmission of SIVcpz from chimpanzees in southeastern Cameroon (22229120). The 'slept with' and 'one person took it around the world' details are his caricature. The speaker is plainly ridiculing the account, which would make this REFUTES + SUPPORTED (section 9 rule 2); it is left UNCLEAR because the rejection is carried entirely by sarcasm.

claim_text: if you start taking these medications, what does this do to your immune system? It lowers your immune system. It compromise your immune system even more
notes: The systematic review of immune recovery on potent antiretroviral therapy (9660367) documents rising CD4+ and CD8+ counts and qualitative immune improvement after viral suppression: the opposite of the claim.

claim_text: babies' brains, the blood brain barrier is not fully formed until six months
notes: Textbook physiology. The review 'The myth of the immature barrier systems in the developing brain' (29528501) presents evidence 'that fetal and newborn brains are well protected'. Medium confidence: barrier function does mature, but not in the sense claimed.

claim_text: do not buy this water for your babies. It is very dangerous ... This water has fluoride ... You do not want babies drinking water with fluoride
notes: Also on screen throughout ('Do NOT Buy This Water for BABIES'). Infant formula made with fluoridated water is associated with mild enamel fluorosis (19571048, summary OR 1.8, 'weak' evidence of causation). The 2025 IQ meta-analysis (39761023) found inverse associations that were null below 1.5 mg/L overall but persisted in low-risk-of-bias studies. Bottled 'baby' water is low in fluoride, and 'very dangerous' is far stronger than any of this. Nothing retrieved contradicts it either, so it is not MIXED (section 7 needs good studies pointing both ways): weak, partial support for a much stronger claim is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE (strength of inference), with the two studies kept as that partial support.

claim_text: Some people believe that fluoride is good for your teeth if you put in the water that's basically been disproven
